name: Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians
land_summary: The Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians are Anishinaabe and Métis people of the Turtle Mountains on the Canadian border in north-central North Dakota. The band's ancestors used a broad stretch of northern Dakota; the 1863 Old Crossing Treaty began the loss of Red River Valley land. An executive order of December 21, 1882, set aside a large reservation, but on March 29, 1884, a second order returned all but two townships to the public domain, opening the best farmland to homesteaders. In 1892 the McCumber Agreement, later called the Ten-Cent Treaty, gave up the band's claim to millions of acres for $1 million. Congress approved an amended version in 1904. With too little land on two townships, many members took allotments on public land elsewhere, including near Trenton, North Dakota, and in Montana. The band holds about 72,000 acres on and around the reservation in Rolette County, plus 6,698 acres near Trenton. Its tribal college was chartered in 1972.

timeline.event: The Old Crossing Treaty begins the cession of Chippewa land in the Red River Valley of northern Dakota.
An executive order of December 21 withdraws a large tract in northern Dakota Territory for the Turtle Mountain band.
A March 29 executive order returns all but two townships (162 and 163 north, range 71 west) to the public domain.
In the McCumber Agreement, later called the Ten-Cent Treaty, the band cedes its claim to millions of acres for $1 million.
Congress approves an amended McCumber Agreement (33 Stat. 194), and members are allotted land, many on public domain away from the reservation.
The tribe charters Turtle Mountain Community College.

notes: tmbci.org was not fetched, per the brief. The nation's current site, tmchippewa.com, loads but has no history, land or acreage text, so homelands is null. The ND Indian Affairs Commission page returned an error. The 1882 order's size conflicts: TMCC and Prairie Public say 22 townships, while ND Studies says 20 townships (460,800 acres). The timeline uses 22. The McCumber Agreement's day also conflicts: TMCC gives October 22, 1892, and OSU's Kappler catalog gives October 2, so only the year is used. TMCC dates the 1904 approval to April 21. That day is single-sourced and was left out. The acreage cession is also inconsistent: TMCC says about 10 million acres in one place and more than 8 million in another, and ND Studies says about 9 million, so the record says 'millions of acres.' The land base figures (72,255 acres on and around the reservation in Rolette County, and 6,698 at Trenton) come from TMCC and ND Studies. ND Studies' own table gives a 140,107-acre total, which likely includes allotments in Montana and elsewhere. There is no nation-published figure. Claims awards were left out because they conflict: TMCC gives $47.3M (1980) plus $4.9M, and Prairie Public gives $52.5M (1982, to the Pembina Band). The 1932 constitution (Wikipedia only) was also left out. No source names T.R. in connection with the 1904 approval, so he is not mentioned.
